overview: The atlas’s “Tukular Caliphate” is the Umarian or Toucouleur state associated with al-Hajj Umar Tall and his successors. Its nineteenth-century conquests brought different communities under changing rulers. Ségou’s library and treasury preserve unusually concrete evidence of scholarship, craft, warfare and the repeated seizure of wealth.

periods.title: Umar’s expansion toward the Niger
periods.summary: The 1859 to 1861 campaign brought Ségou into Umar’s state; it depended on military skill, supply and coercion.

periods.title: Ahmadu at Ségou
periods.summary: Ahmadu inherited and enlarged his father’s library while ruling from Ségou. Other territories and commanders did not form a simple uniform system.

periods.title: French conquest and continuing resistance
periods.summary: France captured Ségou and its treasury in 1890; the dismantling of the wider state continued into 1893.

sections.title: A library was part of the state’s wealth

items.text: Umar began collecting manuscripts by about 1841. After his death in 1864, his son Ahmadu continued enlarging the collection. The BnF describes 518 bound volumes, mostly gathered into a consecutive manuscript series.

The library was seized during France’s conquest of Ségou in 1890 and transferred to Paris. Later binding and cataloging changed its physical organization. Its survival is therefore also a history of conquest and displacement, not simply a peaceful museum acquisition.

Cataloging this material required researchers from several countries. The 1985 inventory and microfilming made the contents more accessible. Scholarship can help reconnect a dispersed collection with the African history from which it was removed.

“رماح حزب الرحيم” means “Lances of the party of the Merciful.” These are the opening words of Umar al-Futi’s Arabic book title, preserved in a 1876 Tunis edition catalogued by Tunisia’s national library. The printed edition is later than Umar’s lifetime, not his original manuscript.

The Treasure of Ahmadu includes ornaments of gold, silver and leather, dated to the late 1700s or early 1800s. Many objects were older than the Umarian state itself. Their survival shows the work of earlier craftspeople as well as later royal collecting.

Umar had seized precious objects from the treasuries of Tamba, Kaarta, Bamana Ségou and Masina. French troops later removed the collection from Ahmadu’s palace. The same object can tell more than one story of conquest.

A famous sabre long connected with Umar offers a warning about labels. The Musée de l’Armée now explicitly calls that attribution false. Its return to Senegal does not prove that Umar personally carried it.

sections.title: Work, families and the cost of campaigns

items.text: Before Umar’s conquest, the Middle Niger around Ségou already supported grain and cotton production and river commerce. Somono boat crews carried goods between routes bringing salt, cattle and horses from the north and products from farther south. The new rulers entered an existing economy.

The 1859 to 1861 campaign needed practical specialists: carpenters repaired gun carriages and smiths made cannonballs. Military technology relied on craft knowledge and maintenance, not merely possession of imported weapons.

Women and children accompanied the army, including relatives and enslaved dependants. When supplies became inadequate at Markoya, Umar ordered many back west. Robinson describes the resulting hunger and remembered suffering. These families were part of the story, although they rarely led the armies.

The checked collection records do not establish how every family ate, treated illness or used toilets. Books and royal ornaments illuminate particular institutions; they cannot stand in for an excavated ordinary household.

sections.title: A political ending, not a vanished people

items.text: French forces took Ségou in 1890, ending Ahmadu’s rule there. Resistance and other power centers continued afterward; Person’s chronology places the wider dismantling in 1893. The map’s 1914 endpoint should not be read as evidence of an independent state surviving to that year.

ending.text: French conquest removed Ahmadu from Ségou in 1890 and dismantled the wider state during the following years. Its communities and religious traditions continued. The library’s surviving manuscripts record intellectual life that cannot be reduced to the political map’s final date.

sources.title: Yves Person: Samori, chronology
sources.note: Scholarly chronology reproduced by web Mande; early 1860s rise, 1892 migration, 1896 to 1897 eastward state, capture 29 September 1898 and death 1900. One treaty date in transcription is inconsistent; not used.

sources.title: David Robinson: The Holy War of Umar Tal, chapter 7
sources.note: Clarendon Press, 1985, chapter reproduced by webPulaaku. Segu campaign of 1859 to 1861, farming, river commerce, artisans and civilian suffering.

sources.title: BnF: Bibliothèque de Ségou authority record
sources.note: Collection begun by Umar from 1841 and inherited and enlarged by Ahmadu after 1864. Contains 518 volumes; at the BnF since 1892. Languages: Arabic and Fula.

sources.title: Review of the Inventory of the Umarian Library of Ségou (1986)
sources.note: Bulletin critique des Annales islamologiques 3, p. 136: library seized 1890, bound 1898 to 1901, international cataloging and microfilm.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Selections from the Treasure of Ahmadu
sources.note: Gold, silver and leather ornaments from the late eighteenth or early nineteenth century. Taken from earlier treasuries by Umar and from Ahmadu’s palace by France in 1890.
